title: Like the earth
hook: the God-conscious one is like the earth, dug by some, anointed by others, the same to both

segments.voice: Yesterday, kamal: in the pond all its life, and the water rolls off. Your line: untouched, like the lotus. Did anything roll off today? The same stanza keeps painting. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

Stand in a field and think about what the ground under your feet puts up with. A farmer drives a plow through it. Someone digs a well, a grave, a foundation. Someone else kneels and plants a rose, or pours fragrant oil on it at a shrine. Rain pounds it. Children run on it. And through all of it, the earth does the same thing it always does. It holds everything up, and it grows whatever is put into it. It doesn't sulk at the plow or preen at the perfume. Guru Arjan saw a portrait of a person in that.
screen: `A PLOW, A WELL, A GRAVE.` → `A ROSE, FRAGRANT OIL.` → `THE EARTH DOES THE SAME THING.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of ashtpadi eight keeps painting. After the lotus and the sun, a third picture: the brahm giaanee looks on all alike, as the wind blows the same on king and beggar. Raaj is the king, rank the poorest of the poor. The wind doesn't check who it's touching. Then the fourth: brahm giaanee kai dheeraj ek. The God-conscious one has one, steady patience, jio basudhaa, like the earth. Basudhaa is an old name for the earth. Kou khodai, kou chandan lep: one person digs it, another anoints it with sandalwood paste. And the earth is the same to both. Sandalwood paste is what you'd smear on something precious, something honored. So the picture stretches as far as it can: one person tears into you, another honors you, and you don't change. Notice it's not saying the earth doesn't notice the plow. It's saying the earth doesn't become a different earth depending on who's standing on it. That's dheeraj, patience, steadiness. The stanza closes with a last picture: this is the brahm giaanee's quality, the way it is fire's natural nature to burn. Not forced. Just what fire is. Lotus, sun, wind, earth, fire. Every picture in this stanza is nature, doing what it does, the same for everyone. And every one is a way of saying: equal treatment, flowing from who you are, not from who's in front of you.
screen: `THE WIND ON KING AND BEGGAR.` · `BASUDHAA: THE EARTH THAT HOLDS.` · `ONE DIGS, ONE ANOINTS.` · `STEADY, LIKE FIRE'S NATURE.` · then, large: `LIKE THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: treat two people the same. Think of two people you'll meet today, one who usually treats you well and one who doesn't. Picture each in turn. Notice how your body changes: maybe you open up for one and brace for the other. Now picture yourself as the ground under both of them. Steady. Holding. The same. Breathe in, feeling your weight on the floor. Breathe out, letting both faces rest on you equally. Later, give them both the same greeting. The bell holds the time.
Basudhaa, the earth. Dug by one, anointed with sandalwood by another, and the same to both.
Your line: the same to both. Today, greet the person who's hardest for you exactly the way you'd greet the easiest. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a picture of steady, equal treatment of everyone, an ideal also lived in the gurdwara, where all sit and eat together as equals.

fork.setup: one person digs into the ground; another anoints it with sandalwood. what does the earth do?
options: gives more to the one with sandalwood.
fork.reveal: jio basudhaa kou khodai kou chandan lep: the God-conscious one's patience is like the earth's.

original.note: Gurmukhi: basudhaa, the earth; the brahm giaanee's patience is like it.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience means putting up with people.
what it means: it's being the same ground for everyone, the digger and the one with sandalwood.
what a scholar hears: basudhaa comes from Sanskrit vasudhaa, an old name for the earth; the stanza closes on fire's sahaj subhaao, its natural disposition.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): review no longer says 'two more pictures' (the stanza has three more: wind, earth, fire); transliteration 'kooo' corrected to 'kou'; the 'literally the one who holds treasure' etymology cut from the teach and the original note.

Lines paraphrased: brahm giaanee kai drisat samaan / jaise raaj rank kau laagai tul pavaan; brahm giaanee kai dheeraj ek / jio basudhaa kou khodai kou chandan lep; Nanak jio paavak kaa sahaj subhaao. Confirm all are pauri 1 of ashtpadi 8 and the transliteration.
